function_question: How does nature stay on top of water?

opening.text: There was a boy called Max who lived in a small village at the edge of a thick jungle.
Max walked 3 hours to school, because a huge river cut right across his path and the only way was the long way round.
Max stopped on the riverbank and thought:

thought.big: What if I could cross right here?
thought.small: School would be minutes away, not hours!

guide.brief: I'm PopAI, your story guide. Max has started thinking about what he could do. What about you? Can you help him? Let's start!
guide.your_idea: Some engineers already have a spark of an idea. Do you?
guide.nature_clues: Nature solved this millions of years ago. Tap each card to meet four nature heroes that are great at staying on top of water!
guide.design_secret: Here's the secret all four heroes share…
guide.skill: Scientists predict before they test. Which boat shape will hold the most coins?
guide.sketch: Time to draw your crossing like a real engineer!
guide.build_and_test:
You started with a first idea. You may have sketched it, built it, or both.
Now you have another possibility—or an improved version of your original idea. You can build and test this version too.
Engineers repeat this cycle: develop an idea, build, test, learn, and improve.
guide.retry_tip: Engineers don't stop after the first round. When they want to understand the effect of a change, they change one thing and test again.
guide.ending: From that day on, Max uses your solution to cross the river and reaches school in just a few minutes. Other people in the village need a solution like this too.

quick_check.question: Crossing the river takes 10 minutes. How much time does Max save each morning?

quick_check.wrong: Not quite. Try 3 hours take away 10 minutes.

discovery.choose_hero_text: You've discovered some amazing ways nature stays on water. Now choose the hero you like most to help Max solve his problem.

partner_lessons.secret: A water strider can stand and run on top of a pond without sinking.
partner_lessons.how: Its legs are covered in very fine, water-repellent hairs. Together with the surface tension of water (the surface acts like a thin, stretchy skin) and its weight spread out over long legs, the water bends under each leg but does not break. This only works because the insect is tiny and light.
inspiration: What if Max designed a lightweight object with special water-repellent supports that spread its weight across the water?
partner_lessons.your_turn: What could you design for Max using the water strider's idea? What would it look like, and what would you make it from?

hint.text: Look closely at the water strider’s legs. They are long, light and water-repellent, so its weight is spread out and the water’s surface only bends under them.
hint.ask: What could you create that spreads weight out over the water in a similar way?

partner_lessons.diagram_alt: A close-up of a water strider leg: tiny water-repellent hairs dent the water surface without breaking it.

partner_lessons.secret: When a flood comes, fire ants hold on to each other and float together as a living raft.
partner_lessons.how: They connect their legs and bodies into one group. Their bodies repel water, and air gets trapped between them, so the whole group stays afloat. One ant on its own could not do this for long.
inspiration: What if Max built a raft from many small pieces that connect together, just like fire ants forming a floating group?
partner_lessons.your_turn: Which small pieces could you connect for Max, and how would you join them? Try a pattern of your own.

hint.text: Look closely at how the ants connect. When many ants join together, small spaces between their bodies can trap air and their connected structure helps them stay on the water.
hint.ask: What could you create that uses lots of connected parts or trapped air in a similar way?

partner_lessons.diagram_alt: One fire ant alone on the water, then many ants linked into a floating raft with air between them.

partner_lessons.secret: The giant water lily has a huge, wide leaf that lies flat on the river and can hold a surprising load.
partner_lessons.how: Under the leaf is a strong network of ribs that branch out like a web. The ribs reinforce the leaf and spread the weight across its wide surface, while the leaf stays lightweight.
inspiration: What if Max designed a wide floating platform with a network of lightweight supporting ribs underneath, just like the giant water lily?
partner_lessons.your_turn: What shape would your platform be, how would you arrange its supports, and what would you build it from?

hint.text: Look under the giant water lily’s leaf. A network of strong ribs supports the wide, light leaf and spreads the load across it.
hint.ask: What could you create that uses a wide surface with a light supporting network in a similar way?

partner_lessons.secret: A coconut can float across the sea for months and still grow into a new palm tree.
partner_lessons.how: Its thick, fibrous husk is full of tiny spaces that trap air. That trapped air helps it float, and the husk cushions and protects the seed inside.
inspiration: What if Max designed a floating platform with lightweight, air-filled spaces inside it, inspired by the coconut's fibrous husk?
It could become a raft, a floating shoe, or a protective floating structure.
partner_lessons.your_turn: Imagine your own structure for Max. Where would the air go, and which materials would you use?

hint.text: Look inside the coconut’s husk. Its fibres hold many tiny air spaces, which help it float and protect what is inside.
hint.ask: What could you create that holds lots of small air spaces inside in a similar way?

companions.title: Zoom in on a leg
steps: A water strider's long legs rest on top of the water.
Closer: each leg presses a small dent into the water's surface, but doesn't break through.
Closer still: thousands of tiny hairs trap air and repel water.
companions.takeaway: Water striders use surface tension: the water's surface acts like a thin, stretchy skin. Their light bodies and water-repellent leg hairs dent that skin without breaking it. This only works because they are tiny and light; it would not hold up something as heavy as a person.
companions.hint: Look closely at its legs and how they meet the water. Which feature might be useful? Remember: what works for a tiny insect may not work at human size.

companions.title: Link the ants
steps: Tap each ant to link it to the group.
companions.takeaway: Fire ants link their bodies together. As a group they trap air and spread out on the water, which helps the colony stay afloat during a flood. One ant on its own cannot do this for long.
companions.hint: Look at how the ants connect. What becomes possible when small parts work together?

companions.title: Look under the leaf
steps: Flip the leaf to see underneath.
Tap each rib to trace the network.
companions.takeaway: This is the Victoria water lily, also called the giant water lily. Under its huge leaf, a network of strong ribs reinforces it and spreads the weight across its wide surface, so the leaf stays flat on the water while staying light. Most water lilies are much smaller and cannot hold large loads.
companions.hint: Look underneath the leaf. How does its supporting network help it hold its shape? Where could your idea need support?

companions.title: Peel back the layers
steps: Smooth outer skin: it keeps water out.
Thick, fibrous husk: full of air spaces, it helps the coconut float and cushions it.
Hard shell: it protects the seed inside.
The seed: after a long journey, it can grow into a new palm tree.
companions.takeaway: An intact coconut's thick, fibrous husk holds lots of air. It helps the coconut float and protects the seed on long journeys across the sea.
companions.hint: Look at the intact coconut's outer layers. How do they help protect it during a journey on water? Which of those functions could matter for Max?
